summary: For 5–6 year olds, teach the diet labels herbivore, carnivore and omnivore by sorting familiar animals into three groups and giving a reason based on what each animal actually eats, not by rote definition. Make the omnivore category central (bear, pig, human, chicken) because children over-simplify it, use the child's own mixed diet as the anchor example, and build in deliberate surprises (fierce-looking herbivores like gorilla/hippo, small carnivores like shrew) to break the 'fierce means meat-eater' rule. Diet is the rule; teeth shape (flat grinding vs sharp pointed) is a supporting clue that bridges toward later teeth and food-chain topics.
misconceptions: 'Big, fierce or with big teeth = carnivore' — sorting gorillas, hippos or elephants as meat-eaters by appearance.
'Omnivore means the animal can't decide / eats anything including non-food' rather than 'eats both plants and animals'.
Assuming all farm/pet animals are herbivores, or that humans are herbivores/carnivores rather than omnivores.
Equating 'carnivore' with 'predator/hunter' only, missing scavengers and small insect-eaters.

activities.title: Feeding-time sorting bench
steps: Place each animal from a queue into one of three troughs: herbivore (leaves), carnivore (meat), or omnivore (both).
Start with easy cases — rabbit to plants, lion to meat — then meet the designed surprise: a gorilla.
After each placement, look at the revealed evidence (the animal's actual meal and/or a teeth close-up) and say the reason aloud: 'the rabbit is a herbivore because it eats grass'.
Sort 'human' and discover a plate of both salad and chicken, then place bear and pig alongside to define omnivore as 'eats both'.
activities.insight: An animal's diet group is decided by what it actually eats (and clued by its teeth), not by how big, fierce or scary it looks; omnivore means 'eats both plants and animals', not 'undecided'.

activities.title: Sort real picture cards in class
steps: Lay out picture cards of at least six familiar animals and three labelled hoops or trays: herbivore, carnivore, omnivore.
Match each animal to a 'what it eats' card (rabbit–grass, lion–meat, bear–berries+fish) and place it in the matching group.
Say a spoken reason for each decision based on the food, e.g. 'the bear is an omnivore because it eats berries and fish'.
activities.insight: Classifying is a justified decision: each animal belongs in a group because of the food it eats, and that reason can be stated out loud.

activities.title: Who eats what — reveal scene
steps: Tap an animal in a scene to reveal its diet group, food examples, and a close-up of its teeth.
Explore the reveals grouped by the three labels to meet exemplars of each category.
After exploring, predict a new animal's group before tapping to check.
activities.insight: Each label (herbivore, carnivore, omnivore) names a real group of animals with characteristic foods and teeth that you can observe.

activities.title: Guess the animal's diet from its day
steps: Listen to or read a short first-person account from an animal describing only the kinds of food it usually eats ('Every day I spend the morning grazing on grass...').
Name the animal's diet group and say the reason drawn from the meals described.

Respond to a follow-up matched to the account: if the animal eats only one kind of food, say what other kind of food an omnivore would also eat; if the account already described both plant and animal foods, name it an omnivore and say why.
activities.insight: You can infer a diet category from evidence of what an animal usually eats, without seeing how the animal looks.

activities.title: Spot the surprise (checking questions)
steps: Answer: an elephant is enormous but eats only plants — what group is it in?
Answer: what do we call an animal, like a bear, that eats both berries and fish?
Answer: are you a herbivore, carnivore or omnivore, and how do you know?
Answer: two animals are the same size — can one be a carnivore and one a herbivore? How would you tell them apart?
For each animal shown, choose the reason that fits — 'eats plants', 'eats meat', or 'eats both' — including a gorilla, where 'eats meat' is the tempting-but-wrong fierce-appearance choice.
activities.insight: Size and fierceness do not determine diet group; you decide by what the animal eats, and humans are animals who are usually omnivores.

checkQuestion: A rabbit and a lion — which is the carnivore and which is the herbivore, and how do you know? Then tell me: is a big scary animal always a carnivore?
checkAnswer: The lion is a carnivore because it eats meat (other animals); the rabbit is a herbivore because it eats plants. You decide by WHAT the animal eats, not by its size or how scary it is — some big animals, like elephants and cows, are herbivores, and some small animals are carnivores.
